title: Reading News
intro: First week back: Michael Morpurgo's memoir lands mid-month, Oxford Reading Tree turns forty, the first Children's Booker shortlist is coming, and reading enjoyment has gone up for the first time in five years.

items.headline: The Worst Witch is a finished series — eight books, 1974 to 2018
items.author: Jill Murphy
items.book: A Bad Spell for the Worst Witch
items.summary: Mildred Hubble is still the most-read thing across our schools, and it is worth telling a Year 3 or 4 class that the series is complete: eight books, from The Worst Witch in 1974 to First Prize for the Worst Witch in 2018, two per school year across Mildred's four years at Cackle's Academy. Jill Murphy wrote and illustrated every one of them, and since her death in 2021 the eight are the whole story. For a child who worries about starting something that never ends, that finished shelf is the selling point.

items.headline: Oxford Reading Tree turns forty this year
items.author: Roderick Hunt
items.summary: Roderick Hunt MBE and illustrator Alex Brychta created Biff, Chip and Kipper in 1986, and Oxford University Press is marking the fortieth year of Oxford Reading Tree in 2026. OUP puts the reach at more than 30 million children learning to read with it. Your schools log Hunt mostly at the early levels, which is exactly where he belongs — and four decades of children following the magic key makes an easy assembly if you want to mark it.

items.headline: For the child who only reads football, Rob Childs is still in print
items.author: Rob Childs
items.summary: Childs taught in Leicestershire and ran school football, cricket, athletics and cross-country before The Big Match came out in 1987 and let him write full time — which is why his matches read like someone who has actually stood on a touchline. He has written more than seventy books, over fifty of them about football, and Penguin still carries The Big Match, Soccer Mad and the County Cup books. Short, quick and built for the child who has decided reading is not for them, which is a decision that tends to get made in the first weeks of a new year.

items.headline: Michael Morpurgo's memoir of the farm behind War Horse is out on 17 September
items.author: Michael Morpurgo
items.summary: Down Burrow Lane: Life and Love on the Farm is Morpurgo's account of the fifty years he and Clare have spent on a remote Devon farm — the one behind War Horse, Private Peaceful and Farm Boy, which your readers are on now. He was a young schoolteacher when they moved there, and the charity they started, Farms for City Children, has since brought more than 100,000 children from towns and cities to the countryside. Hodder & Stoughton publish it in hardback at £20 on Thursday 17 September. One for the staffroom rather than the book corner, but it is the story behind the books the children are reading.

events.name: Roald Dahl Story Day, his 110th birthday
events.blurb: Dahl was born on 13 September 1916, so this is the 110th. It falls on a Sunday, which makes Friday the 11th the practical day to do something about it; the official site has free lesson plans for key stages 1 and 2.

events.name: Julia Donaldson's birthday
events.blurb: Born 16 September 1948, and still the safest bet in any infant classroom. Three days after Roald Dahl Story Day, if you would rather run one story week than two separate things.

events.name: National Poetry Day
events.blurb: Thursday 1 October, and this year's theme is Wonder. The National Literacy Trust has free classroom resources ready to go, which is usually enough to build a morning around.

events.name: Michael Morpurgo's birthday
events.blurb: Born 5 October 1943, so he turns 83 a fortnight after Down Burrow Lane comes out. A neat excuse to put War Horse or Farm Boy in front of an upper key stage 2 class.

events.name: First Children's Booker Prize shortlist announced
events.blurb: Eight books for 8 to 12-year-olds, announced on Tuesday 24 November. It arrives in good time to be a ready-made class reading list for the spring term, with the winner following on 2 February.

events.name: World Book Day 2027
events.blurb: Thursday 4 March. A long way off, but it goes in the diary now because the £1 book list and the costume panic both arrive sooner than anyone expects.

general.label: Reading research
general.text: Reading enjoyment has risen for the first time in five years: 36.1% of children and young people said they enjoyed reading in their free time in 2026, up from 32.7% in 2025, across 125,375 pupils aged 5 to 18. The catch for primary schools is that 5 to 8-year-olds were the one age group to go backwards, from 62.6% to 61.6%.
general.source: National Literacy Trust, Annual Literacy Survey 2026

general.label: Reading news
general.text: Patrice Lawrence MBE is the fourteenth Waterstones Children's Laureate, handed the medal by Frank Cottrell-Boyce at the Barbican on 7 July 2026 and in post until 2028. Her theme is the power of stories to build communities, which sits neatly alongside this term's National Year of Reading focus.

general.label: Reading news
general.text: The first Children's Booker Prize, for fiction aimed at 8 to 12-year-olds, is chaired by Frank Cottrell-Boyce. The winner takes £50,000 and each of the eight shortlisted authors £2,500, and three children aged 8 to 12 sit alongside the adult judges to pick the winner. Shortlist on 24 November 2026, winner on 2 February 2027.

general.label: Worth knowing
general.text: The National Year of Reading runs under the banner Go All In, and the autumn term theme is reading in the community — schools working with families and their local library rather than carrying it alone. The National Literacy Trust's school toolkits and webinars are free, and you can join partway through.
